description: Authored rationale for the HU single-raised-pot river nodes (S7): the third-barrel/value-bet decision (hero = flop+turn aggressor) and facing a river bet (hero = flop+turn caller). Keyed by hero/counterpart pairing; scoring itself lives in backend/app/domain/postflop.py (grade_river_barrel / grade_vs_river_bet). Source: docs/research/02-postflop-strategy.md §5.

rationale_parts.lead: The river is where value discipline gets paid: they've called two bets, so a third needs a clear answer to 'what worse hand calls?'
points: Strong hands bet and size up — river bets are polar (very strong or bluff), and a caller who came this far pays off with their bluff-catchers.
Marginal made hands check back and take the free showdown: after two calls they mostly get called by better and fold out worse.
Busted draws are the natural bluffs — but only on scare rivers that keep your story believable, never as an automatic third bullet on a blank.

rationale_parts.lead: After barreling twice from the cutoff, the river is mostly a value question — your arriving range is strong, so the skill is judging thin value.
points: Bet big and polar with hands that beat their bluff-catchers; check back the marginal pairs whose showdown value dies the moment a third bet goes in.
If the river completes the flush or straight they called two streets to chase, give up without key blockers.
If it pairs the board or brings an overcard, your story since the flop stays believable — the barrel keeps its fold equity (chance they fold).

rationale_parts.lead: A third barrel from UTG is the most value-heavy line in the game — so make yours look exactly that way.
points: Bet strong hands for value at a size worse hands can still call.
Resist thin value: after calling twice, their range is condensed around exactly the pairs that beat a marginal holding.
Bluff only with a busted draw AND a scare river that hits your narrow range harder than theirs; on blanks and draw-completers, checking and giving up is the profitable discipline.

rationale_parts.lead: Facing the button's third barrel, start from the pot odds: the bet size tells you exactly how often your call must win — that number, not the feeling of being bluffed, is the decision.
points: The button's wide range produces the most missed draws of any seat, so on blank rivers where the draws all bust, calling with decent pairs keeps its value.
On scare rivers that complete draws or pair the board, their story is believable — folding a bluff-catcher at a bad price is correct.
A busted draw of your own has zero showdown value: it's never a call — only a fold (or a rare raise-bluff you shouldn't make by default).

rationale_parts.lead: A cutoff river bet after two barrels leans value: the same bluff-catcher that calls a button barrel can be a fold here.
points: Price first: a small bet needs your hand to win rarely; a pot-sized bet needs about one win in three.
Then ask whether the cutoff's line even contains enough natural bluffs (missed draws) to clear that bar — it has fewer than the button's.
Strong hands call or raise for value; marginal pairs call selectively on blanks and fold on the scare rivers; no-showdown-value hands just fold and save the bet.

rationale_parts.lead: Three bets from UTG at live stakes is almost always a real hand — this line is badly under-bluffed, so your price must be exceptional before a pure bluff-catcher calls.
points: Do the arithmetic anyway: the bet size sets the winning percentage your call needs.
If their line realistically holds almost no missed draws, a marginal pair doesn't clear the bar at any normal size.
Call with strong hands and your best bluff-catchers on blank rivers; fold the rest without regret — losing the minimum against an under-bluffing player IS the edge.
